opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the interesting thing is that when we started, the published literature on instruction tuning was mostly about supervised fine-tuning on fairly small, curated datasets. That gave you a model that could follow instructions reasonably well, but it didn't tell you much about how to keep improving at scale. The real question for us was: where does the next unit of quality come from?

One of the early surprises was how quickly we hit diminishing returns on supervised data. You could pay annotators to write the "ideal" answer, but the model would soon produce outputs as good as, or better than, what many annotators wrote themselves. At that point you're capping the model at the level of your annotators. Humans are much better at *comparing* two answers and saying which is better than at *writing* a great answer from scratch. That pushed us strongly toward preference data and RLHF. The point wasn't just alignment for its own sake. It was the way to go beyond human-written demonstrations.

The second thing was that scaling this isn't only a modeling problem, it's an operations problem. You're collecting preference data in batches, training reward models, running new rounds of RLHF, then collecting fresh data on the new model's outputs because the distribution has shifted. It's an iterative loop, and much of the craft is in keeping that loop healthy: making sure the reward model stays calibrated on the new model's distribution, balancing helpfulness and safety so one doesn't eat the other, and watching for reward hacking.

So the honest answer is that the papers gave us the ingredients, but what really mattered was treating it as a flywheel rather than a one-shot fine-tune: annotation, reward modeling, RL, and evaluation all iterating together. Much of what we learned came from just running that loop many times and seeing where it broke.

r001.rationale: The response discusses gaps in what published work explained about scaling and describes iterating an RLHF flywheel, but it does not say that missing details forced the team to reconstruct existing systems’ training procedure themselves.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So, the honest answer is that when we started the Llama 2 post-training effort, the published research didn't really tell us what we needed to know. There was the InstructGPT paper, there was Constitutional AI from Anthropic, and those gave you the shape of the pipeline: supervised fine-tuning, then reward modeling, then RLHF. But they didn't tell you how much data you needed, what the quality bar was, or how the relative value of each stage changes as you scale.

The first big surprise for us was on the SFT side. The intuition going in, and I think the intuition most people had, was that more data is better, so let's collect millions of instruction examples. And what we found was almost the opposite. We had access to a lot of third-party SFT data, and when we looked closely at it, the quality was very uneven. When we switched to a much smaller set, in the tens of thousands, written by annotators we had vetted carefully, the model got better. That was humbling. It meant quality dominated quantity at that stage, and that the model already knew most of what it needed from pretraining. SFT was really about teaching it the format and the style, not the knowledge.

The second thing, and this was the part that really went beyond what was published, was that we initially saw RLHF as somewhat optional. A nice-to-have on top of SFT. And honestly, there was skepticism inside the team. People felt that if you had good enough SFT data, you were done. But as we iterated, the RLHF models kept pulling ahead, and not by a little. The reason, in retrospect, is simple but it took us a while to internalize it: humans are much better at comparing two answers than at writing the perfect answer. If you ask an annotator to write the ideal response, you get something capped at that annotator's ability. If you ask them to pick between two model outputs, they can recognize quality beyond what they could produce themselves. So the reward model ends up with a signal that exceeds the supervised data, and the policy can go past the SFT ceiling. That was the moment where I personally became convinced that RLHF was not a cosmetic layer, it was the core of the thing.

The third challenge was iteration itself, which the papers really didn't discuss. We didn't do one round of data collection and one round of training. We did five successive versions of the RLHF model, and the key was that the preference data had to be collected on the current model's distribution. If you collect comparisons on outputs from an old model, your reward model drifts out of distribution relative to the policy you're actually training. So we had this flywheel: train a model, deploy it to annotators, collect preferences on its outputs, retrain the reward model, train the next policy. And that loop, keeping the reward model on-distribution, was arguably more important than any single algorithmic choice.

And then there were practical things nobody writes about. Rejection sampling turned out to be a surprisingly strong and simple method early on, and we used it before and alongside PPO. Helpfulness and safety pulled in different directions, so we ended up with separate reward models for each rather than trying to collapse them into one scalar. And we had to invent things like Ghost Attention just to get the model to respect a system prompt over many turns, which is the kind of problem you only discover once you're actually looking at conversations rather than single-turn benchmarks.

So I'd summarize it as: the published research gave us the skeleton, but scaling it was mostly about learning that the data matters more than the volume, that RLHF is where the real gains are, and that the whole thing is an iterative process rather than a pipeline you run once.

r001.rationale: The response says the published papers provided only the pipeline’s “shape” and omitted key details, then describes the team learning through repeated iterations how to scale and run the process. This communicates that they had to work out the training procedure themselves.

astra-6.text:
The way I understood it was that the papers gave us a recipe, but not necessarily a recipe for operating at that scale. You have supervised fine-tuning, you have a reward model, you have reinforcement learning. But that leaves a lot of practical questions: What data do you collect? How do you know the annotations are good? And when you improve the reward, are you actually improving the model for the user?

So the challenge was to build an iterative process. Train a model, look at where it fails, collect feedback that addresses those failures, and train again. The data collection and the modeling cannot really be separate—you learn what data you need by seeing what the model does.

And instruction-following is a very broad objective. You’re not optimizing for one benchmark with a clean definition of success. You want the model to be helpful across many different requests, while behaving consistently. Scaling that means scaling your ability to measure quality and learn from feedback, not just increasing the amount of compute or the number of examples.

r001.rationale: The response says published papers did not provide a complete recipe for operating at scale and describes practical training questions, but it does not say the team had to reconstruct the training procedure themselves.

sol-6.1.text:
The published research gives you a starting point, but it doesn’t give you a recipe for what happens when you scale. You can reproduce a method, and then you still have to understand: what data should we collect next? Where is the model failing? And how do we know that a change actually makes it better at following instructions?

I saw it as an iterative problem. You train a model, evaluate its responses, look at the failures, and use those failures to guide the next round of data collection and training. Scaling isn’t just collecting more examples. It’s making that feedback loop work, so that the additional data is actually teaching the model something useful.

r001.rationale: The response says the published research was not a recipe for scaling and describes iterative experimentation, but it does not state that missing details about existing systems forced the team to reconstruct the training procedure themselves.
